en: If he had not found that counsel,
Would the forty companions not seize and slaughter him?
Would they not cut off his head like a sheep’s,
Would they not split his belly like a melon?
There was no help to be had from Baychoro,
Your sister-in-law Kanykey had no recourse.
Below Tört-Kül,
In the garden Lord Manas had planted,
At the dark eye of the spring,
Right beside the plane tree,
Stood Khan Manas’s great palace.
They surrounded the great palace tightly,
Raising the battle cry “Köbösh!” in a clamor,
Readying their spears,
Preparing their battle-axes,
Baring their tusks,
Their swiftest horses drawing apart,
Smoothing their fine mustaches,
Their strongest men coming into view.
The forty companions struck by the spirits
Broke away and went in front.
When the sun sank wavering,
When the first of the people lay down,
When dawn came shining forth,
When light fell upon the earth,
The rear of dawn swelling,
The sun emerging bright and round,
Stars scattering from the sky,
Dispersing toward the qibla,
As dawn split and opened,
Khan Manas’s forty companions
Drew their bows like falling rain,
Shot their arrows like hail.
“Seize, seize, seize them!
If you seize them, bind them!”
Köbösh came in shouting.
Dust rose from his movement;
That swine’s voice drove the soul away.
His face was like greased wheat,
His eyes like twilight mist.
“Seize them, my people, seize them!” he said.
“The one she keeps as her refuge,
Her colt Semetey—kill him!” he said.
“The orphan she relies upon,
Let us seize him now.
And Chyyyrdy, whom she takes as support—
Let us tear her up for the great dogs!
Among women, the one who wrecks the people,
That bitch of a woman Kanykey—
Let us take our revenge like this!”
When they came covering the place in a mass,
Your dear mother Kanykey
Remained entirely unconcerned.
The six scoundrels charging in with shouts
She did not rate equal to her trouser cuff.
Kanykey, built like a warrior,
Your nobly born white hawk,
Your white hawk simply stood there,
Your poor tigress.
Without looking aside, your sister-in-law Kanykey,
Your poor champion stood there.
Smashing and ravaging the palace—
May God strike those dogs!
That fierce leopard, your sister-in-law—
If you looked where she sat,
It was passing through her lung.
The forty companions left by Manas—
How could those forty companions be stopped?
Pouring arrows like rain,
Once they had all rushed in together,
They knocked down all the buildings,
They felled all the willows.
From Khan Manas’s palace,
How much delight they took!
The countless riches left by your Khan Manas,
Those huge dogs divided, measuring with a whip.
While the leopard khan was alive,
The one with gates of iron and steel,
Beijing of the Khakan—
When he was besieging it,
Taking much tribute in gold coins,
He had gathered an abundant treasury.
To the child left young without a father,
A treasury he would give to the orphan;
To the woman parted from her husband,
A treasury he would give to the widow;
To those who had lost both eyes,
A treasury he would give to the blind;
To those without hands or feet,
A treasury he would give to the disabled.
They plundered those riches now;
The six slaves wrought havoc in earnest.
A whole otter skin
They split in half,
And those dogs used it to trim their trouser cuffs.
Shaggy as a slave whose master had died,
His nose bulging like a leather bottle,
Climbing a hill and bellowing,
Calling the battle cry “Köbösh!”
The place where leopard Manas died,
The countless riches left by the blood-shedding hero—
The place where scoundrels divided them by whip lengths!
The white-marked horses on the hills,
Thoroughbreds and fleet steeds mingled—
They came raiding those too.
Swaggering at their ease,
The forty companions and six scoundrels
Grew rich by dividing it among themselves.
They had seven gelded camels fitted with packsaddles.
Andijan cloth with silk weft, yellow-patterned,
Precious black-patterned cloth from Bukhara—
They loaded these and departed.
They had six hundred gelded camels fitted with packsaddles.
Red gold, countless gold coins,
Ruby stones that had come from China—
They loaded these up.
Ten thousand sheep filling the pasture,
Countless tethered camels—
They drove them all away.
Thus they brought utter ruin.
That beauty among the dark-complexioned,
That radiant one among the poor Muslims,
Your leopard sister-in-law Kanykey,
Was left there alone,
Parted from her blood-shedding hero
At thirty-two years of age.
Lord Manas, the blood-shedding hero,
Had not been dead forty days.
Upon her great dark head,
Her bloody face torn,
She sat steadfast beneath the mourning effigy.
The child she was to raise,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Stood nursing, rigid and still,
Gripping Aktinte and bracing herself,
The blood drained from her face and she grew ashen.
To the child she was nursing,
Slave Köbösh came without hesitation:
“As a married woman, you overturned custom and ruined the people;
As a maiden, you shook the age and ruined the nation.
Your swift steed, which you would not give when asked—
Bitch, have I cast my grim catching pole upon it?!
The ruby stones you would not give when begged—
Have I seized them before your eyes!
Was your Manas more of a hero than I?
Is Köbösh inferior to Manas?!
‘When a horse dies, its rump hide is wanted,’ they say;
‘When an elder brother dies, his widow is wanted,’ they say.
If an intermediary comes, you slaughter him.
An envoy who comes between us,
You beat for no cause.
You wretched bitch, you will come to no good!
Your blood-shedding Manas is no longer here,
Yet you will not give up your defiance!
You will not understand an intermediary’s words.
We and Manas share a father—
Born of the elder wife and the younger wife,
Yet you will not marry any one of us!
Where the wild duck flies and never returns,
Is Kara-Kyr your open plain?
Black-faced woman who means to flee,
Do you intend to go to your own kin?
The renowned champion you rely upon—
Is that renowned Bakai your lion?
The one you would flee toward and marry—
Is Ormombek, Tekechi’s son, your husband?
The orphan left by Manas
You have kept only as a pretext.
Bitch, you have turned your thoughts to another.
The one you keep as your support,
The one who will utterly crush me—
Is that your infant in the cradle?”
Roaring, he took Arkesken,
Drew it into his hand.
The dogs began their uproar;
The swaddled child
He cut into six pieces!
“Here, if you will not marry me, fierce woman!” he said.
A black-bladed battle-axe
He seized and swung.
At the cartilage of the right shoulder blade,
Your formidable, unfortunate mother—
He struck her then.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Cried out weeping and fell doubled up.
When Köbösh drew back and struck,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Then fell straight upon her head.
When she cried “Oh!” from her mouth,
Your sister-in-law’s blood came in heaving gushes.
Losing consciousness, her eyes rolling,
A night of ruin fell upon her.
Her forehead bone was sloping;
She was destined to see this horror.
When the hero’s eyes had closed,
Your sister-in-law’s days were ill-starred.
The hair at her nape was grass;
When the hero’s eyes had closed,
Your poor, fierce sister-in-law
Had many calamities to bear.
When slave Köbösh struck her down,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Lay embracing the earth.
As he was about to take her apple-like head,
As he was about to cut your sister-in-law up for the great dogs,
Slave Shuutu, with a felt cap like a yurt covering,
Manas’s close companion,
Seized Köbösh:
“Köbösh, you are no khan, you are worthless!
If you truly are a khan,
How could you cut off a woman’s head?!”
Exceptionally mighty hero Shuutu
Now spoke in varied ways.
Your dear, fierce sister-in-law—
Preventing Khan Köbösh from striking her,
He rescued your sister-in-law.
Her tongue did not speak; she said no word.
Your sister-in-law had lost her speech.
Taking no rest day or night,
Your sister-in-law lost her looks.
Unable to find a way to move,
Your sister-in-law lost her strength.
Darkness deepened before her eyes,
A day of trouble fell upon her burdened head.
Her rib bones split apart,
Her blood poured from her side.
For a day and a night,
She lay unconscious.
At midmorning,
She came to her senses.
It had driven the poor woman from her wits:
They had cut in two
The very child she had been nursing.
When she raised herself and looked,
There was no bluff where she could hide,
There was no food she could swallow.
There was no support on which she could rely,
There was no place where your sister-in-law could take cover.
There was no forest into which she could flee.
To anyone she might take as shelter,
There was none who would not bear her ill will.
Unable to collect herself,
A day of hardship fell upon her.
Upon your precious sister-in-law’s head
Fell a night no human should witness.
“My leopard lord, do not die!” she said.
“Let this wretched soul not see sorrow!” she said.
“If God creates someone as a living soul,
To any woman after me,
God, do not give such horror!” she said.
“My dear long, thick braid,
When my blue-maned lord died,
My poor head fell to plunder like this.
Winding my silken hair six times,
Why did I not braid it?
His fine mustache flattened,
